mainTopic: Oaths about a מצוה versus optional matters, and the rules of repeated oaths not to eat a loaf: how many times one is liable, which wording forbids what, and what happens when an oath is annulled.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא of רבי יונתן. It then shows that the rule 'a שבועת ביטוי applies only to optional matters' can also fit רבי יאשיה, who follows רבי עקיבא's method of רבויי ומיעוטי. The limiting words of the verse must leave out something, and that only works if the verse is about דבר הרשות. Next the גמרא discusses רבי יהודה בן בתירא, who holds one is liable for an oath about a מצוה. He points to oaths to do good to others, and the חכמים answer that such an oath still has a valid negative form ('I will not do good'), while a מצוה does not. A new משנה then teaches that swearing several times not to eat a loaf makes one liable only once, and it lists the penalties for שבועת ביטוי and שבועת שוא. Using רבא's rule that 'I will not eat' forbids any כזית while 'I will not eat it' forbids only the whole loaf, the גמרא explains why the order of the oaths matters. It also explains that an extra oath still exists and takes effect if the first is annulled. A suggested proof from two נזירות is rejected. Finally, רב אחא בריה דרבא challenges רבא's rule about annulling an oath on a loaf while a כזית remains, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of רבי יונתן's rule: separate unless the verse says 'together'
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of רבי יונתן in the ברייתא: a verse listing two items applies to each one alone, unless the Torah writes 'together'.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...until the verse spells out for you 'together'.
steps.whatsHappening: We are catching the last words of רבי יונתן's statement in a ברייתא quoted just before this. He says that when a verse lists two things, it means each one alone, unless the verse writes 'יחדיו' (together).
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יונתן, a list like 'his father and his mother' covers both together and each one separately, without needing any extra word. Only the word 'יחדיו' would limit it to both together. The גמרא had used this to show that its derivation fits רבי יונתן, since for him 'להרע או להיטיב' can easily mean each one alone.

phrases.english: until the verse spells out for you "together."
phrases.notes: These are the last words of רבי יונתן in the ברייתא. A verse that says 'together' is 'לא תחרש בשור ובחמר יחדו' (דברים 22:10).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted earlier on the דף, which tied the derivation to רבי יונתן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For רבי יונתן, two items listed in a verse apply even separately, unless the verse says 'יחדיו'.

steps.title: The derivation can fit רבי יאשיה too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the derivation can even follow רבי יאשיה, because he holds like רבי עקיבא's method of רבויי ומיעוטי, so the word 'או' is free to separate the items.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say it follows רבי יאשיה. He agrees with רבי עקיבא, who learns using 'adding and limiting' (רבויי ומיעוטי), so the word 'or' is left over for him to separate the items.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says we don't have to say the derivation follows only רבי יונתן. It can follow רבי יאשיה too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יאשיה needs a word like 'או' (or) to show that two listed items apply separately. One might think he has no spare 'או' here. The גמרא answers that he learns this verse the way רבי עקיבא does, with רבויי ומיעוטי, so the 'או' in 'להרע או להיטיב' is extra and can teach that each item counts on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: rules of 'adding and limiting'; רבי עקיבא's method of reading verses
to separate, to treat each item on its own

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'או' is not used for רבויי ומיעוטי. Since רבי יאשיה gets his רבוי and מיעוט the way רבי עקיבא does, the 'או' is a spare word, and he uses it to separate the items.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows Rabbi Yoshiya;
and he holds like Rabbi Akiva,
who learns from additions and limitations,
so the word "or" is left over for him to separate.
phrases.notes: This is the 'או' in 'להרע או להיטיב' (ויקרא 5:4).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the earlier claim. The derivation does not have to follow רבי יונתן only.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the other תנא also has a spare word to learn from.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only רבי יונתן could learn that 'להרע או להיטיב' applies to each item alone, because רבי יאשיה has no spare word.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יאשיה follows רבי עקיבא's method, so the 'או' is free to separate the items, and the derivation fits him as well.

steps.title: The verse must be about optional matters
steps.stepSummary: If the verse is about optional matters, the limiting words exclude a מצוה. If it were about a מצוה, there would be nothing left to exclude.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense if you say the verse is about an optional matter, because then it limits and leaves out a matter of מצוה. But if you say it is about a matter of מצוה, what would it be leaving out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows why the verse of שבועת ביטוי must be talking about optional matters (דבר הרשות) and not a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבי עקיבא's method, a limiting phrase (מיעוט) must leave something out. If the verse is about דבר הרשות, the מיעוט leaves out דבר מצוה, which makes good sense. If the verse were about דבר מצוה, the מיעוט would have nothing to leave out, so that reading cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: it makes sense if you say
an optional matter, not commanded or forbidden
a matter the Torah commands or forbids
from what? what is left out?

steps.whatToRemember: שבועת ביטוי is about optional matters. The limiting words in the verse leave out oaths about a מצוה, and that only works if the verse is about דבר הרשות.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the rule that an oath to do or not do a מצוה is not a שבועת ביטוי. The rest of the discussion about רבי יהודה בן בתירא builds on it.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא בִּדְבַר הָרְשׁוּת כְּתִיב,
phrases.english: It makes sense if you say it is written about an optional matter,
it leaves out a matter of מצוה;

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּדְבַר מִצְוָה כְּתִיב,
phrases.english: but if you say it is written about a matter of מצוה,
what is it leaving out?
phrases.notes: This is not a real question. The point is that the limiting words would have nothing to leave out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא בִּדְבַר הָרְשׁוּת כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how רבי עקיבא's method of רבויי ומיעוטי (now also רבי יאשיה's) proves the verse is about optional matters.
steps.raayaObject: That the verse of שבועת ביטוי is about דבר הרשות.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rule that a מיעוט must leave something out. Only דבר הרשות leaves something (דבר מצוה) for it to exclude.

steps.title: Quoting רבי יהודה בן בתירא from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה's opinion of רבי יהודה בן בתירא, who argues with a קל וחומר that one is liable for an oath about a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירא said: If for an optional matter... (and so on, as in the משנה).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting רבי יהודה בן בתירא from the משנה. This line sets up the comment that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יהודה בן בתירא argues: if one is liable for an oath about an optional matter, which he was never sworn to at הר סיני, he should surely be liable for an oath about a מצוה, which he was already sworn to at הר סיני. This disagrees with the rule just learned, that שבועת ביטוי is only about optional matters.

keyTerms.meaning: if this is so... then surely; the opening words of a קל וחומר
short for וכולי, 'and so on': the rest of the quote is in the משנה

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira said:
If for an optional matter, etc.
phrases.notes: The full argument is in the משנה: if one is liable for an optional matter, surely he is liable for a מצוה, which he was already sworn to at הר סיני.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא מָה אִם הָרְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the derivation from the verse to the next opinion in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה בן בתירא holds, using a קל וחומר, that one is liable for breaking an oath about a מצוה.

steps.title: The חכמים's reply to רבי יהודה בן בתירא looks strong
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the חכמים's answer to רבי יהודה בן בתירא in the משנה is a strong argument. This raises the question of how he could still hold his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים argued well against רבי יהודה בן בתירא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the חכמים's reply in the משנה is a very good point. This sets up the next question: how can רבי יהודה בן בתירא still hold his opinion?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the חכמים answered him: an oath not to do a מצוה does not take effect, so an oath to do a מצוה should not make one liable either. The גמרא calls this argument correct, which seems to leave רבי יהודה בן בתירא with no answer. The discussion that follows has to explain his side.

keyTerms.meaning: they are saying it well, their point is correct

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not the final ruling. It praises the חכמים's argument in order to ask how רבי יהודה בן בתירא would answer it.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis argued well to him,
phrases.notes: The argument is in the משנה: an oath not to do a מצוה does not take effect, so an oath to do a מצוה should not make one liable either.

phrases.english: to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן שַׁפִּיר קָאָמְרִי לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the opinion just quoted by pointing out that the חכמים's reply seems to defeat it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה בן בתירא's קל וחומר that one is liable for an oath about a מצוה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Turn the oath around: an oath not to do a מצוה does not take effect, so an oath to do a מצוה should not make one liable either. His קל וחומר seems to fail.

steps.title: רבי יהודה בן בתירא answers with the case of doing good to others
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירא says the 'both directions' test is not required. The Torah includes an oath to do good to others even though an oath to harm others is not included. In the same way, it can include an oath to fulfill a מצוה even though an oath to neglect a מצוה is not included.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירא can answer: Isn't it true that doing good to others is included by the Torah, even though harming others is not? So here too, fulfilling a מצוה is included, even though neglecting a מצוה is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 5: how can רבי יהודה בן בתירא keep his view after the חכמים' strong argument? He brings a case that shows the Torah includes some oaths even when their opposite does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים argued that an oath only counts if it could work in both directions, the way an oath about optional things can (I will eat / I won't eat). רבי יהודה בן בתירא points to the פסוק's word 'להיטיב'. It includes doing good to others, even though an oath to harm others does not count. So the 'both directions' rule cannot be a strict requirement.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah (literally 'the Merciful One') included it

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא אָמַר לָךְ:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira could say to you:
Is it not so that doing good to others —
phrases.notes: This comes from the word 'להיטיב' in the פסוק about oaths, ויקרא 5:4.

phrases.english: even though it is not
matched by harming others,
phrases.notes: He means an oath to harm others does not count, yet the opposite, doing good to others, does.

phrases.english: the Merciful One still included it?
Here too, with fulfilling a מצוה —

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֵיתֵיהּ בְּבִיטּוּל מִצְוָה,
phrases.english: even though it does not apply to neglecting a מצוה,
the Merciful One included it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא אָמַר לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 5 by defending רבי יהודה בן בתירא against the חכמים' argument.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example: a case the Torah includes even though its opposite does not count
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An oath counts only if it could work in both directions, so an oath about a מצוה is excluded.
steps.terutzMaskana: Doing good to others shows that working in both directions is not required, so an oath to fulfill a מצוה can count.

steps.title: The חכמים explain why doing good to others is different
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer that doing good to others can still be flipped into the valid oath 'I will not do good'. A מצוה cannot be flipped into 'I will not fulfill it'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים? There, the oath works for 'I will not do good'. Here, does an oath work for 'I will not fulfill a מצוה'?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how the חכמים would push back against רבי יהודה בן בתירא's proof. They say his example is not the same as a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The right way to flip 'I will do good to others' is 'I will not do good', not 'I will harm others'. That negative oath is valid, so doing good to others really does work in both directions. A מצוה has no valid negative form, because one cannot swear not to fulfill it, so it stays excluded.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I will not do good' (the negative form of an oath to do good)
The Rabbis (the חכמים of the משנה)

steps.whatToRemember: The חכמים' test is whether the oath has a valid negative form. Doing good to others has one ('I will not do good'), but a מצוה does not, so an oath about a מצוה is not a שבועת ביטוי according to them.
steps.confusionAlert: The opposite of 'doing good' here is NOT 'harming', but simply 'not doing good'. That is the whole point of the חכמים' reply.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
There, it works with 'I will not do good';
here, does it work with 'I will not fulfill'?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the counter-example of Step 6 by showing it does have a valid negative form.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the comparison between doing good to others and fulfilling a מצוה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The true negative of 'doing good' is 'not doing good', which is a valid oath, so that case does work in both directions. A מצוה has no valid negative form.

steps.title: Swearing three times not to eat the same loaf
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: if someone swears three times not to eat a certain loaf and then eats it, he is liable only once.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'An oath that I will not eat this loaf'; 'An oath that I will not eat it'; 'An oath that I will not eat it'; and then he ate it — he is liable only once.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches what happens when a person repeats the same oath several times and then breaks it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three oaths forbid the very same act, eating this loaf. Once the first oath takes effect, the later ones add nothing, because a prohibition cannot take hold where one already exists. So eating the loaf makes him liable for only one oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (written in the text as מַתְנִי׳)

phrases.english: MISHNA:
'On my oath, I will not eat this loaf';
'On my oath, I will not eat it';
'On my oath, I will not eat it';
and then he ate it —
he is liable only once.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל כִּכָּר זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the debate about oaths on a מצוה has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Repeating the same oath about the same act creates only one liability.

steps.title: The penalties for breaking a שבועת ביטוי
steps.stepSummary: The משנה explains that this kind of oath is a שבועת ביטוי. Breaking it on purpose brings מלקות, and breaking it by accident requires a קרבן עולה ויורד.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a שבועת ביטוי, for which one gets מלקות if he breaks it on purpose, and brings a קרבן עולה ויורד if he breaks it by accident.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה names the kind of oath it has been discussing and lists its penalties.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath like 'I will not eat this loaf' is a שבועת ביטוי, a personal oath about one's own actions. The penalty depends on intent: מלקות for breaking it on purpose, and a קרבן עולה ויורד for breaking it by mistake. That offering is called 'rising and falling' because its cost depends on what the person can afford.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath of utterance: a personal oath to do or not do something
A 'sliding-scale' offering whose cost depends on the person's wealth

steps.whatToRemember: A שבועת ביטוי brings מלקות if broken on purpose and a קרבן עולה ויורד if broken by mistake. Repeating the same oath still counts only once.

phrases.english: This is an oath of utterance —
for which one is liable to lashes for breaking it on purpose,
and for breaking it by mistake, a sliding-scale offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה by naming the type of oath and its penalties.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Breaking a שבועת ביטוי on purpose brings מלקות; breaking it by mistake requires a קרבן עולה ויורד.

steps.title: The penalty for a vain oath
steps.stepSummary: The משנה closes with the rule for a שבועת שוא: lashes if sworn on purpose, no penalty if sworn by accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: For a שבועת שוא, a person who swears it on purpose gets מלקות. A person who swears it by accident is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its list with one more kind of oath, the שבועת שוא, and states its penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Compare this with step 9. A broken שבועת ביטוי done by accident requires a קרבן עולה ויורד. A שבועת שוא done by accident has no penalty at all. Only the on-purpose case is punished, with מלקות.

keyTerms.meaning: A vain oath: an oath that is plainly false or pointless

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 9. There, an accidental שבועת ביטוי brings a קרבן. Here, an accidental שבועת שוא brings nothing at all.

phrases.english: An oath in vain –
one is liable to lashes for swearing it on purpose,
and for swearing it by accident, one is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא חַיָּיבִין עַל זְדוֹנָהּ מַכּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה's list of penalties, setting the vain oath beside the שבועת ביטוי from step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שבועת שוא: lashes if done on purpose, exempt if done by accident.

steps.title: Why does the משנה use two different wordings?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה words the first oath 'I will not eat' and the next one 'I will not eat it'.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why did the משנה need to say the first oath as 'I will not eat' and the next one as 'I will not eat it'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks about the exact wording of the משנה's case of repeated oaths from step 8. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה could have repeated the same words each time. Instead, it switched from 'I will not eat' to 'I will not eat it'. The גמרא wants to know what that change teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it to teach? The גמרא is asking about the משנה's wording

phrases.english: GEMARA: Why do I need it to teach
'An oath that I will not eat' (this loaf),
phrases.notes: This is the first oath in the משנה from step 8: 'I will not eat this loaf.'

phrases.english: and then 'An oath that I will not eat it'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the case of repeated oaths about the loaf (step 8) and asks about its wording.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the change from 'I will not eat' to 'I will not eat it' teach?

steps.title: The order of the oaths decides how many times he is liable
steps.stepSummary: The wording teaches that 'I will not eat' followed by 'I will not eat it' gives one liability. The reverse order gives two.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us that he is liable only once because he said 'I will not eat' first and then 'I will not eat it'. But if he said 'I will not eat it' first and then 'I will not eat', he would be liable twice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה chose its order on purpose. The order is what makes him liable only once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's ruling of 'only one liability' depends on the order of the oaths. If the order were reversed, the second oath would take effect, and he would be liable twice. The next step explains why.
steps.confusionAlert: Both orders use the same two phrases, yet the result is different. Only the order changes the outcome.

phrases.english: This teaches us:
the reason is that he said 'I will not eat'
and then said 'I will not eat it' –
that is why he is liable only once;
but if he said 'I will not eat it'
and then said 'I will not eat' –
he is liable twice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 11 about the משנה's wording.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wording shows that the ruling of one liability depends on this order. In the reverse order, he is liable twice.

steps.title: רבא: 'I will not eat' means any bite, 'I will not eat it' means the whole loaf
steps.stepSummary: The answer follows רבא. 'I will not eat this loaf' is broken by eating one כזית. 'I will not eat it' is broken only by eating the whole loaf.
steps.simpleTranslation: This follows רבא, who said: if someone swears 'I will not eat this loaf', he is liable as soon as he eats a כזית of it. If he swears 'I will not eat it', he is not liable until he eats the whole loaf.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind the answer in step 12 by quoting רבא's rule about what each wording forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'I will not eat' forbids every כזית, so it already covers the whole loaf. A later 'I will not eat it' adds nothing new and has no effect. In the reverse order, 'I will not eat it' only forbids the whole loaf. A later 'I will not eat' adds a new ban on each כזית, so it takes effect and gives a second liability.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with the view of רָבָא
The size of an olive, the smallest amount that counts as eating
Until he eats all of it

steps.whatToRemember: A broad oath ('I will not eat': no bite at all) covers a narrower one ('I will not eat it': not the whole loaf). So the narrow oath coming second adds nothing. The broad oath coming second adds a new ban, so it counts.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general idea: a second oath only takes effect if it adds a new ban beyond what the first oath already forbade.

phrases.english: This follows רבא, as רבא said:
'An oath that I will not eat this loaf' –
once he has eaten an olive-sized amount of it, he is liable.
'That I will not eat it' –
phrases.notes: Saying 'it' points to the loaf as one whole thing, so the oath is about eating all of it.

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיֹּאכַל אֶת כּוּלָּהּ.
phrases.english: he is not liable until he eats all of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind step 12's answer by quoting רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'I will not eat this loaf' is broken by eating one כזית. 'I will not eat it' is broken only by eating the whole loaf.

steps.title: Why mention the third oath?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of a repeated 'I will not eat it' and asks why the משנה needs to mention this extra oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'On my oath I will not eat it,' and then he ate it, he is liable only once. Why do we need this extra oath mentioned?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line in the משנה and asks why it bothers to list another 'I will not eat it' oath. That rule seems obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 already taught that 'I will not eat' followed by 'I will not eat it' gives only one liability. So adding a third, identical oath seems to teach nothing new. The גמרא wants to know what this extra line adds.

phrases.english: "On my oath I will not eat it," and he ate it —
he is liable only once, etc.
Why do I need this additional one?
phrases.notes: He means the extra, repeated 'I will not eat it' oath, which seems to add nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's wording after the discussion of רבא's rule about 'this loaf' versus 'it'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is taught by the משנה listing an additional identical oath?

steps.title: No extra liability, but the oath is still there
steps.stepSummary: The extra oath brings no extra punishment, but it is a real oath that takes effect if it finds room.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us: there is no extra liability, but there is an oath. If you find room for it, it takes effect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the extra oath teaches something new. It is not empty. It is a real oath waiting in the background.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Liable only once' could make us think the repeated oaths are meaningless. The משנה's wording shows they are only blocked from adding punishment. If the first oath ever disappears, the extra one has 'room' and kicks in.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what it teaches us

steps.confusionAlert: 'Liable only once' does not mean the later oaths are void. They exist, but they add nothing while the first oath is in force.

phrases.english: This teaches us:
it is liability that there isn't —
but an oath there is;
so that if you find room, it takes effect.
phrases.notes: 'Room' means a situation where the extra oath has something left to forbid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra oath is a valid oath without extra liability, and it takes effect whenever it has room.

steps.title: When does this make a difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a practical case where the extra oath's 'room' would matter.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what law does this matter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where we would ever see the extra oath take effect. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying the oath 'exists' is abstract. The גמרא wants a real situation where the result changes because of it.

phrases.english: For what law does this matter?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical application of step 15's principle.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what case does the extra oath actually take effect?

steps.title: רבא: if the first oath is annulled, the second takes its place
steps.stepSummary: The difference shows up in רבא's rule: annul the first oath, and the second one takes effect instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: It matters for רבא's rule. רבא said: if he asked a חכם to release him from the first oath, the second oath takes effect in its place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical case. It is רבא's rule about annulling the first of several oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a חכם releases the first oath (התרת שבועה), it is as if it never existed. Now the second oath has 'room', so it takes effect and the person is still bound.

keyTerms.meaning: asked a חכם to annul a vow or oath

steps.whatToRemember: A repeated oath adds no punishment, but if the first oath is annulled, the next oath takes over (רבא).
steps.whyThisMatters: Someone who annuls only his first oath is still forbidden, because the later oath now applies.

phrases.english: For the rule of רבא —
as רבא said:
that if he asked for release from the first one,
phrases.notes: 'Asked' means he went to a חכם to have the oath undone.

phrases.english: the second one takes effect for him in its place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by naming רבא's rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: If the first oath is annulled, the second takes effect in its place.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא: after the first oath is annulled, the second oath takes effect in its place.

steps.title: A possible proof from two נזירות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a ברייתא about two נזירות supports רבא: once the first is annulled, the term already kept counts for the second.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this supports him? Someone vowed two נזירות, kept the first term, and set aside a קרבן for it. Afterward he asked a חכם to annul the first one. The days he kept count for the second.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a source that seems to back רבא's rule. This time the case is about נזירות instead of oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the first נזירות is annulled, the second נזירות is treated as having been in effect all along. So the term he already kept counts as the second, and he does not need to keep another one. That looks just like רבא's idea that the second commitment steps into the first one's place.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say this supports him?

steps.confusionAlert: 'לימא' means 'shall we say'. It is only a suggested proof, and the גמרא may still reject it.

phrases.english: Shall we say this supports him:
one who vowed two nazirite terms,
and counted the first
and set aside an offering for it,
and afterward asked for release from the first —
the second counts for him through the first.
phrases.notes: The days he already kept now count as the second term, so he is finished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a suggested support for רבא's rule from step 17.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's rule that annulling the first commitment lets the second take its place
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about someone who vowed two נזירות and annulled the first after keeping it

steps.title: The two נזירות are not like two oaths
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the ברייתא. A second נזירות exists on its own, but a second oath on the same thing has no standing at all while the first one is still in place.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them?! There, the second נזירות is real no matter what. Once he finishes counting the first term, he has to go back and count the second one, even without asking a חכם for anything. Here, is there a second oath at all?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from Step 18 and shows that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two נזירות stack one after the other, so the second one is a real obligation even if nobody annuls the first. A second oath not to eat the same loaf adds nothing while the first oath stands, so it only 'exists' if the first is removed. That means the ברייתא cannot prove that annulling a first oath wakes up a second one.

keyTerms.meaning: 'How can you say that?!' — a phrase that rejects a comparison
at any rate, in any event
counts (the days of the נזירות term)

phrases.english: How can these be compared?!
There, the second naziriteship exists in any event,
for once he counts the first term,
he needs to go back and count the second
even with no request to annul.
phrases.notes: In other words, even if he never goes to a חכם, he still owes the second נזירות.

phrases.english: Here, the second oath —
does it exist at all?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the ברייתא. רבא's rule itself is not rejected.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The cases are not alike: a second נזירות is independently real, while a second oath has no standing unless the first is removed.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא of two נזירות does not prove רבא's rule, because a second נזירות is real on its own and a second oath is not.

steps.title: רבא: you can annul an oath on a loaf only while an olive-bulk remains
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone swore about a loaf and then ate it, he can still ask to annul the oath if he left an olive-bulk. If he ate the whole loaf, he can no longer ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone swore about a loaf and then ate it, he can ask a חכם to annul the oath as long as he left over an olive-bulk of it. If he ate the whole loaf, he can no longer ask to annul it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule from רבא about when a person can still ask to annul an oath after eating the thing he swore about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא makes the right to annul depend on how much of the loaf is left. If a כזית remains, annulment is still possible. Once the whole loaf is gone, it is not.

keyTerms.meaning: an olive-bulk, the standard minimum amount for eating
asks (a חכם) to annul the oath about it

phrases.english: Rava says:
If one took an oath about a loaf and ate it —
if he left over an olive-bulk of it,
he may ask to have the oath about it annulled;
if he ate all of it,
he may not ask to have the oath about it annulled.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא נִשְׁבַּע עַל כִּכָּר וַאֲכָלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching of רבא about annulling an oath after eating.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person can ask to annul an oath about a loaf only if at least a כזית of it is left. Once the whole loaf is eaten, annulment is no longer possible.

steps.title: Which oath wording could רבא mean?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רב אשי what case רבא is talking about. If the oath was 'I will not eat,' the first כזית was already a sin. If it was 'I will not eat it,' why does it matter that exactly a כזית was left?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, the son of רבא, said to רב אשי: What is the case? If he said 'I will not eat,' then he already broke the oath with the very first olive-bulk he ate! If he said 'I will not eat it,' why mention specifically an olive-bulk?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בריה דרבא challenges רבא's rule by trying both possible oath wordings and showing a problem with each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'I will not eat,' every כזית is forbidden, so the sin already happened with the first bite and leaving a כזית does not change that. With 'I will not eat it,' only eating the whole loaf is forbidden, so any amount left over should be enough, and a full כזית should not be needed. Either way, רבא's mention of a כזית seems hard to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
'that I will not eat' — forbids even a כזית
'that I will not eat it' — forbids only eating the whole thing
Why specifically this? Why single this out?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi:
What are the circumstances?
If he said: 'I will not eat' —
phrases.notes: Earlier in the sugya, רבא read this wording as forbidding even one כזית of the loaf.

phrases.english: with the first olive-bulk he already committed his transgression!
If he said: 'I will not eat it' —
phrases.notes: This wording only forbids eating the whole loaf.

phrases.english: why specifically an olive-bulk?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי הֵיכִי דָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's rule from Step 20 by asking what case it fits.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's requirement that a כזית be left over in order to annul the oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is a two-sided challenge. With 'שלא אוכל' the sin already happened at the first כזית. With 'שלא אוכלנה' any leftover amount should be enough. Neither wording explains why a כזית matters.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two wordings. 'שלא אוכל' forbids even a little, while 'שלא אוכלנה' forbids only the whole loaf. The whole challenge depends on this difference.
